events.title: Cotton fibres in a Neolithic grave at Mehrgarh
events.summary: Threads preserved by mineralization in a copper bead from a Neolithic burial at Mehrgarh were analysed and identified as cotton (genus Gossypium). The authors could not say whether the cotton came from a domesticated species, but wrote that cotton was already known and exploited for its fibres at this period.
events.significance: Cotton, the fibre every later Indus textile and every block-printed cloth in this story depends on, was in use in the Indus region more than 3,000 years before the Priest-King.

sources.title: First evidence of cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh, Pakistan (abstract and commentary)
sources.quote: In this study, several threads preserved by mineralization in a copper bead from a Neolithic burial (6th millennium) at Mehrgarh, Pakistan, were subject to rigorous metallurgical analysis.

sources.title: First evidence of cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh, Pakistan (abstract and commentary)
sources.quote: it seems clear the cotton as such was already known and exploited for its fibres at this period.
sources.note: Year is DERIVED: the page says '6th millennium'; c. 5500 BCE is the midpoint used for the chart. Accessed 2026-11-21.

events.title: The earliest textile evidence at Harappa
events.summary: Excavations at Harappa recovered woven-textile impressions on terracotta beads and spindle whorls from the site's earliest occupations. Harappa.com dates the earliest evidence of textiles there to about 3300 BCE.
events.significance: Spinning and weaving are secure in the Indus world long before the carved cloak of the Priest-King.

sources.title: Harappan Textiles
sources.quote: The earliest evidence of textiles at Harappa goes back to about 3300 BCE, and is another suggestion of how important this product must have been to the later Indus economy.

sources.institution: tDAR (the Digital Archaeological Record): abstract of a paper on Harappan textiles
sources.title: Plant based textiles and basketry at Harappa, Pakistan (3700-1900 BCE)
sources.quote: Woven textile impressed terracotta beads and spindle whorls provide evidence for spinning and weaving from the very earliest occupations at the site during the Ravi Phase (3700-2800 BCE).

events.title: The Priest-King's carved cloak
events.summary: A steatite bust, 17.5 cm high, found at Mohenjo-daro and now in the National Museum, Karachi. Its left shoulder is covered with a cloak decorated with trefoil, double circle and single circle designs that were originally filled with red pigment, cut with a specialized drill and touched up with a chisel. The carving shows a pattern on a garment; it does not show how that pattern was made on cloth. Harappa.com itself puts the name 'Priest King' in quotation marks.
events.significance: The oldest image of a patterned cloth in this story, and the reason for the question the page asks: could such a pattern have been printed?

events.title: A scrap of cotton from Mohenjo-daro, reported dyed with madder
events.summary: John Marshall's excavators found a small piece of woven material on the lid of a silver case, preserved by silver salts. The Technological Research laboratory in Bombay found the convoluted structure characteristic of cotton and called its results 'tentative'. The Ashmolean Museum notes that a cotton fragment from Mohenjo-daro, carbon-dated to 1760 BCE ±115, 'has been reported to show evidence of madder dyeing', which would imply knowledge of mordants. Two cautions: the lab report was preliminary, and 1760 BCE is later than the urban Harappa period.
events.significance: The only reported hint of mordant dyeing in the Indus world. It makes a red, printed cloak possible, not shown.
